m1-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Why GenAI is rewriting careers”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Start with tasks, not a disappearing job title
sections.explanation: A role contains many different tasks. Examine those tasks before deciding where AI assistance belongs.

items.label: Map the work
items.detail: List recurring tasks, stakeholders and consequences before choosing a tool.

items.label: Separate the tasks
items.detail: Distinguish routine drafting from judgement, relationships and authorised decisions.

items.label: Choose assistance
items.detail: Try a bounded draft or comparison that you can independently check.

items.label: Review the result
items.detail: Check accuracy and usefulness before it reaches another person.

sections.takeaway: Keep responsibility with the person even when a draft is machine-assisted.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. AI changes tasks before it changes jobs

sections.title: The augmented graduate’s evidence loop
sections.explanation: Capability becomes visible when a learner can show both the output and the checking behind it.

items.label: Understand
items.detail: Use your subject knowledge to recognise the actual problem.

items.label: Direct
items.detail: Provide a clear brief and relevant authorised material.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check facts, calculations and fitness for the audience.

items.label: Explain
items.detail: Show your contribution, corrections and resulting artefact.

sections.takeaway: An attractive AI output is not proof that its author can verify or explain it.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. The "AI-augmented graduate" is the new entry-level standard

sections.title: Local context is an input, not an assumption
sections.explanation: A useful Indian-language or local-business deliverable needs context the assistant may not possess.

items.label: Language
items.detail: Specify the intended language and check natural wording with a fluent speaker.

items.label: Audience
items.detail: Name the reader’s knowledge, purpose and constraints.

items.label: Local evidence
items.detail: Supply approved documents or observations rather than invented local facts.

items.label: Access
items.detail: Choose an available workflow and an acceptable offline alternative.

sections.takeaway: Ask a knowledgeable local reviewer to check meaning and context; do not treat translation as validation.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Why this matters more in India, not less

sections.title: Three career plays, one evidence standard
sections.explanation: Using AI in a profession, building useful workflows and creating new offerings require different demonstrations.

items.label: Improve your role
items.detail: Show how a checked workflow helps a task in your chosen discipline.

items.label: Build a solution
items.detail: Demonstrate a narrow assistant, automation or app with safe failure handling.

items.label: Create an offering
items.detail: Test whether a specific audience finds the proposed service useful.

sections.takeaway: Choose a concrete problem and evidence of competence, not a fashionable label.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. The three career plays

sections.title: The skills the tool does not take over
sections.explanation: Delegating a draft does not delegate accountability, relationships or the ability to recognise an error.

items.label: Domain understanding
items.detail: Know enough to identify misleading assumptions and wrong answers.

items.label: Human relationships
items.detail: Listen, negotiate and understand needs beyond a written prompt.

items.label: Integrity
items.detail: Disclose assistance and own the claims you submit.

items.label: Learning habits
items.detail: Keep practising the skill instead of only collecting outputs.

sections.takeaway: Your judgement, communication and evidence of learning remain part of every submission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. What does not change

checkpoint.question: Can a polished AI-generated report demonstrate competence on its own?
checkpoint.answer: No. Show how you framed the task, checked the claims, corrected errors and explain your own contribution.

m1-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “AI, ML, deep learning & GenAI — what is actually different”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Read the AI family map as a teaching simplification
sections.explanation: The lesson focuses on modern deep-learning-based generative systems. These labels describe related methods and capabilities, not four stages a user must complete.

items.label: Artificial intelligence
items.detail: The broad field includes rule-based methods as well as learned systems.

items.label: Machine learning
items.detail: Systems learn patterns from examples rather than only hand-written rules.

items.label: Deep learning
items.detail: Layered neural networks learn representations from data.

items.label: Modern GenAI
items.detail: Many current systems generate text or other media using deep neural networks.

sections.takeaway: Many modern GenAI systems use deep learning; generative methods more broadly are not all deep-learning systems.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Four nested circles

sections.title: An answer is assembled one token at a time
sections.explanation: Follow the generation loop. A token can be a word part, a word or punctuation; fluency alone does not verify an answer.

items.label: Read context
items.detail: The system receives the available instructions, conversation and supplied material.

items.label: Predict possibilities
items.detail: The model estimates possible next tokens from the current context.

items.label: Choose and append
items.detail: A decoding procedure selects a token and adds it to the output.

items.label: Continue or stop
items.detail: The updated text becomes context until an ending condition is reached.

sections.takeaway: A plausible next token is not an authoritative fact check, and generated citations still need opening.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. How a language model actually works (the honest, non-mathematical version)

sections.title: Keep the moving parts distinct
sections.explanation: The same chat interface brings together a trained model, temporary context and sometimes tools. They are not interchangeable sources of knowledge.

items.label: Model and training
items.detail: Learned parameters come from training; a cut-off does not establish current knowledge.

items.label: Prompt and context
items.detail: Instructions and available conversation guide this particular response.

items.label: Tokens and window
items.detail: Token limits bound the material a system can consider at once.

items.label: Fine-tuning
items.detail: Additional training changes model behaviour; it differs from attaching a document.

items.label: Tools and modalities
items.detail: Search, actions, images or audio depend on enabled product features and permissions.

sections.takeaway: Attaching a file is context or retrieval, not necessarily retraining the model.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Vocabulary you will use every week

sections.title: Different media, different checks
sections.explanation: Generation can produce several kinds of media. Each needs a review that fits the medium rather than a generic “looks good”.

items.label: Text
items.detail: Verify claims, sources, calculations, audience and wording.

items.label: Images
items.detail: Inspect composition, text rendering, likeness and permission to use the result.

items.label: Speech and audio
items.detail: Listen for pronunciation, meaning, consent and licence conditions.

items.label: Video
items.detail: Review every shot for continuity, misleading edits and accessible captions.

sections.takeaway: Check meaning, rights, accessibility and continuity as appropriate for the output.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Where the other GenAI types fit

sections.title: A powerful pattern learner still needs verification
sections.explanation: Broad language patterns can support useful drafting and explanation. They do not guarantee that a specific answer is true.

items.label: Useful draft
items.detail: Use the model to propose a structure, explanation or alternative.

items.label: Locate claims
items.detail: Separate checkable facts from suggestions and invented examples.

items.label: Check evidence
items.detail: Open primary sources or reproduce the calculation independently.

items.label: Own the final
items.detail: Correct, qualify or reject unsupported material before use.

sections.takeaway: Match the checking effort to the cost of a mistake, not to the confidence of the writing.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Why "just predicting the next word" is not a put-down

checkpoint.question: Does an answer that sounds confident prove that the model looked up a reliable source?
checkpoint.answer: No. It may be generated from learned patterns. Inspect the actual source and verify the specific claim.

m1-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “The GenAI ecosystem: tools, tiers & your starter toolkit”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Choose a tool category before a brand
sections.explanation: Start with the kind of work you need to do. One product can span categories, but its permissions and capabilities still need checking.

items.label: Conversation
items.detail: Draft, explain and compare text with a chat assistant.

items.label: Research
items.detail: Find and organise sources, then open and verify them.

items.label: Visual creation
items.detail: Generate or edit images and design artefacts.

items.label: Video
items.detail: Plan, generate and assemble moving-image content.

items.label: Audio
items.detail: Create or edit speech and sound with consent and rights checks.

items.label: Automation
items.detail: Connect bounded steps, tools and no-code applications.

sections.takeaway: Choose a workflow for the task; do not collect accounts merely because a tool is popular.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. The six categories

sections.title: Compare assistants on the same task
sections.explanation: A fair comparison controls the prompt and input material, then checks the outputs against the same requirements.

items.label: Fix the task
items.detail: Use the same permitted brief and source material.

items.label: Run candidates
items.detail: Record the tool and relevant settings for each attempt.

items.label: Check consistently
items.detail: Judge correctness, constraints and usefulness with the same rubric.

items.label: Log a choice
items.detail: Keep examples and note where each option failed.

sections.takeaway: A preference on one test is not proof that one assistant is universally best.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Choosing a chat assistant

sections.title: Availability and price are not learning outcomes
sections.explanation: Tool limits and plans change. Plan around the required artefact and a viable alternative rather than a promised free feature.

items.label: Needed capability
items.detail: Identify the specific action the exercise needs.

items.label: Access conditions
items.detail: Check age, institution, region, usage and account restrictions.

items.label: Fallback workflow
items.detail: Use an allowed free or offline alternative when the feature is unavailable.

sections.takeaway: Check current limits and terms before signing up or committing a project to a paid capability.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Free tiers, paid tiers and "student" pricing

sections.title: “Open” and “local” answer different questions
sections.explanation: Model availability, execution location, licence terms and data handling are separate properties.

items.label: Model access
items.detail: Check which weights or code are available and under what licence.

items.label: Execution location
items.detail: Identify whether processing happens on a device or a remote service.

items.label: Operational responsibility
items.detail: Review resources, updates, data exposure and who maintains the system.

sections.takeaway: Local execution does not automatically make a workflow safe, lawful or suitable.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Open models and "local" AI

sections.title: Set up the boundary before the first upload
sections.explanation: An account is an access route to data and tools. Configure it deliberately before using course or workplace material.

items.label: Protect access
items.detail: Use a unique password and available multi-factor authentication.

items.label: Review settings
items.detail: Inspect retention, training-use and sharing controls for that account.

items.label: Minimise inputs
items.detail: Use synthetic or approved material and remove unnecessary personal details.

items.label: Keep recovery safe
items.detail: Store recovery information securely and review connected access.

sections.takeaway: Use only authorised material and do not share passwords, credentials or private records in prompts.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Account hygiene from day one

checkpoint.question: Does running an open model locally remove the need for a privacy review?
checkpoint.answer: No. Licence, device security, access, data retention and the sensitivity of the task still matter.

m1-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “Capabilities, limits & responsible use”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Capability and consequence belong on the same map
sections.explanation: A fluent draft, a specialised factual answer and a consequential decision need different levels of supervision.

items.label: Easy to inspect
items.detail: Formatting and a low-stakes draft can often be checked directly.

items.label: Evidence-dependent
items.detail: Facts, calculations and specialist claims need independent verification.

items.label: High consequence
items.detail: Sensitive or irreversible decisions need appropriate authority and human review.

sections.takeaway: Do not move a task into unattended automation just because one demonstration looked convincing.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. What GenAI is good at, unreliable at and bad at

sections.title: Five warning signs are reasons to investigate
sections.explanation: Different failure modes can coexist in the same answer. Read for evidence and context, not only grammar.

items.label: Fabrication
items.detail: A convincing claim or citation may not exist.

items.label: Bias
items.detail: Language or recommendations may treat people unfairly.

items.label: Stale context
items.detail: The response may rely on old or missing information.

items.label: Confident error
items.detail: A forceful tone can conceal weak support.

items.label: Privacy exposure
items.detail: The workflow may disclose material that should never have been entered.

sections.takeaway: A second AI answer can be another error; use an independent check where correctness matters.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Five failure modes to recognise on sight

sections.title: Automate, augment or avoid
sections.explanation: The decision depends on risk, verifiability and permission, not only how much time a tool might save.

items.label: Automate
items.detail: Use only for bounded, low-risk work with clear checks and permission.

items.label: Augment
items.detail: Let AI assist while a knowledgeable person verifies and decides.

items.label: Avoid
items.detail: Do not delegate prohibited, unsafe or unverifiable work.

sections.takeaway: Keep meaningful review where errors could harm a person or an institution.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. The Automate / Augment / Avoid framework

sections.title: Assistance is not authorship permission
sections.explanation: A course’s project policy and an exam’s restrictions can differ. Check the actual rule before using a tool.

items.label: Read the policy
items.detail: Identify what assistance this particular task allows.

items.label: Keep your work
items.detail: Retain your drafts, sources and reasoning evidence.

items.label: Disclose assistance
items.detail: Name the tools and the contributions you accepted or changed.

items.label: Defend the result
items.detail: Be able to reproduce and explain your submission independently.

sections.takeaway: Disclosure does not make a prohibited use permissible; follow the specific assessment rules.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. Academic integrity: the rules in this course and in your degree

sections.title: Responsibility continues after the classroom
sections.explanation: Real use introduces affected people, organisational authority and consequences beyond a good assignment mark.

items.label: Define purpose
items.detail: State who benefits and who could be harmed.

items.label: Review boundaries
items.detail: Check data, rights, institutional policy and applicable requirements.

items.label: Test safely
items.detail: Use permitted examples and include likely failures.

items.label: Monitor and stop
items.detail: Assign an owner and a way to withdraw a harmful workflow.

sections.takeaway: If a safeguard or approval is missing, pause the proposed use rather than assume permission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. Responsible use beyond the classroom

checkpoint.question: If an AI-use statement is present, can you use AI in an exam that prohibits it?
checkpoint.answer: No. Disclosure is not permission. Follow the rules of that particular assessment.
